utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. If there are no procedural matters to raise, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and may God help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye for the Prosecution is now commencing the examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say a few words in French, if you don't mind, very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you prefer to use the French language, that's no problem; we will receive interpretation in the relevant languages. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French, just a few words. I would like to thank you and I would like to apologise because I sent a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt you. We are in public session. If you want to address the problems we had before you came here to the Tribunal, we should go first into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I wanted to apologise for the problems that may have arisen as a result of my letter, and I would like to thank you for your understanding. And I hope that everything will go well. And from now on I will speak in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these words. We will take them into consideration. When you take the floor and answer questions, please don't touch the microphone. Mr. Vanderpuye, it's your turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President. And good afternoon to you, Your Honours, and everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Dr. Petrovic. We met a little bit earlier today, and as you know my name is Kweku Vanderpuye. And on behalf of the Prosecution I will put some questions to you with respect to your testimony today. I just wanted to let you know a couple of things. You've been here before, so you understand that it's important to try to be precise in your answers and also to speak a little bit more slowly than you would otherwise to give the interpreters an opportunity to translate accurately everything that you say. And if there's anything that I ask you during the course of your examination that's not clear, please let me know so that I can rephrase it in a way that we can understand each other a little bit better. I told you a little bit earlier when I met you this morning that your testimony would comprise your prior testimony in the Popovic case as well as some questions that I may put to you with leave of the Court. So let me get started with that. Do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor v. Popovic on the 4th through the 6th of December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I do remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review the entirety of your testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the hotel over the past two days I went through the whole text. I did have the uncorrected version of the text but that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know that we spoke about a couple of things that you wanted to clarify, which we will get to, but having reviewed your testimony, can you confirm that you stand by it and that it accurately and fairly reflects what you would say if you were to be examined and asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender Dr. Petrovic's Popovic testimony. I have it as P1243 under seal and P1244 as well as the associated exhibits that are marked for identification that were used and admitted through the witness and were used with the witness and admitted through other witnesses in the prior proceeding. If you would like me to, I can read them out into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If there are not too many, you should do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President. In addition to P1244 and 1243, I have P1245 through 1248 -- no, sorry, through 1249. And I have P1251 and 125 -- that's it, I think. Yes, just P1251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it you are tendering only one of those admitted into evidence through this witness in the Popovic case, that means P1245?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President. Actually, I see this P1240 -- bear with me for a moment. I have P1245 through P1248 that were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is different. You are tendering all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to all. Exhibit marked for identification P1245 has in the meantime become a Defence exhibit, D117. So perhaps this would be something to take into account so that we don't have duplicates of exhibits in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I received the information from the Registrar that this is indeed the same document. Would you confirm that, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First the transcript of the Popovic case P1243 under seal and P1244 will be received with these numbers. In addition, D117 - I think we should use this number - and P1246 through P1248 will be received exhibits. Mr. Vanderpuye, you indicated that you will tender three of the six used with this witness in the Popovic case but admitted through another witness. Will you use these documents with this witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there are two documents. P1249 and P1251. I misspoke when I said 1252. I don't intend to use P1249 with this witness. I understand that it was used with him in the prior testimony, but it's -- I don't feel that's particularly material for the examination that I am going to conduct now. But I think it is important to have it because it is a part of that testimony, part of the totality of his testimony which will assist the Trial Chamber in understanding it. And P1251 -- just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, P1251 is the road book in this case which refers -- well, provides additional information to orient -- which I think will assist, rather, in orienting the Trial Chamber when it comes to evaluating the video footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a long time ago that we had a 92 bis witness. I think we all forgot the procedure with these documents not admitted through this witness in the prior case. Perhaps you should reconsider your position on that, but I propose that you just go ahead and start your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Petrovic, I mentioned to you, also when we met a little bit earlier today, that the evidence in this case, as I indicated, would comprise your prior testimony, and I do have a brief summary that I'd like to read to the Trial Chamber which, as I indicated, doesn't contain all of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if I may proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In July 1995, Zoran Petrovic was a journalist from Belgrade who was present in and around Srebrenica on 13 and 14 July, 1995. On 12 July, in an effort to cover the emerging story concerning the Srebrenica events, Mr. Petrovic tried but was unable to enter the Republika Srpska from Ljubovija, Serbia, just across the Drina River from Bratunac. He returned to Belgrade and appealed to deputy commander of the Special Police brigade of the Republika Srpska MUP, Ministry of the Interior, Ljubisa Borovcanin for help, which materialised the following day. Mr. Petrovic had known Borovcanin since the winter of 1994 when he met him as an embedded journalist with the Telegraph Weekly, a Belgrade publication, during the Defence of a radio relay system at Mount Majevica. He again met Borovcanin in the summer of 1995. This was several weeks before the Srebrenica operation, and he documented the activities of Borovcanin's unit and their battle with Muslim forces in Semizovac. Mr. Petrovic successfully entered the Republika Srpska on 13 July 1995 at the Ljubovija bridge border crossing, where Borovcanin awaited him. They travelled to Bratunac by car and arrived at the UN compound in Potocari at around 2.30 or 3.00 p.m. Mr. Petrovic recorded video footage of the events occurring in and around the UN compound, and he testified that he was struck by the large number of people who had fled Srebrenica there. He confirmed that he saw piles of items - bags, blankets, and clothing - but denied having seen anyone beaten, maltreated, or abused. He filmed the white house where Muslim prisoners can be seen on the balcony. He asserted that these prisoners were known or suspected criminals but could not identify from where or when he received this information. Mr. Petrovic also filmed the events occurring along the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road as far as the village of Pervani in the direction of Konjevic Polje. He recorded anti-aircraft fire by Serb forces into the hills where the column of Muslim men from Srebrenica had fled, Muslim prisoners detained at Sandici meadow, men and boys that were captured nearby, and the movement and activities of VRS and MUP units along the Konjevic Polje road. He also shot a sequence of the Kravica warehouse showing a pile of dead Muslim prisoners in the foreground of the building. Mr. Petrovic spent the night of 13 July at Borovcanin's apartment in Bratunac. On 14 July, Mr. Petrovic continued to shoot footage featuring Srebrenica town and comprising various interviews he conducted with Serb returnees to the town. He spent a second night at Borovcanin's apartment as well, and left for Belgrade on the morning of 15 July 1995. Shortly after returning to Belgrade from the footage he shot on the 13th and 14th of July, Mr. Petrovic produced a 28 minute documentary entitled "Operation Srebrenica" for Studio B. The film aired on or about the 17th of July, 1995. On the 28th of February, 2006, Mr. Petrovic met with OTP representatives. He provided them with a copy of the raw footage recorded on the original 8 millimetre tape that he used in July 1995. The OTP copied this tape, which was signed by Mr. Petrovic. In his testimony concerning the Studio B material, Mr. Petrovic testified that certain footage was edited as part of the production of the documentary. He worked with two editors in this process. However, he was not able to fully explain why certain sequences that appear in the Studio B material are not found in the raw footage. For example, while the sequence showing Muslim prisoners on the balcony of the white house in Potocari is seen in the Studio B production, is does not appear in the raw footage. Similarly, the Kravica warehouse footage shot on 13th July, 1995, appears in the Studio B footage but does not appear in the raw material. However, Mr. Petrovic stated that he could not remember -- he could not remember this during the course of his testimony. Further, although shot on 13 July 1995, the Kravica warehouse footage appears in the Studio B production interrupting a sequence recorded on 14 July. Mr. Petrovic stated that this anomaly was due to "technical reasons" or, in essence, an aesthetic effect. Mr. Petrovic testified that his ability to film the material at issue was not restricted and that he never discussed the Kravica warehouse footage with Borovcanin. Borovcanin, however, was with him when he -- when the footage was shot, and according to Petrovic the sequence was "the most powerful images he had ever filmed." Mr. Petrovic further testified that he shot the Kravica footage following an incident involving one of Borovcanin's troops. He testified that he heard that one fighter under the command of Mr. Borovcanin whose nickname was Oficir had been wounded, that he had jumped on somebody who had weapons, and that his arms were hurt in that skirmish, and that he had been urgently transported to the hospital in Bratunac. He described the incident in a subsequent article, writing: "At the moment of his surrender, at the corner of the building, a Muslim soldier suddenly jumped on a Serbian combatant, snatched his rifle, and riddled him with a burst of fire. Oficir, one of Ljubisa's - that's Ljubisa Borovcanin's - Special Forces members jumped on him, knocked him down, he was, himself, lightly wounded in the wrestling. Oficir is one of the hopes of Borovcanin's formations, so the commander goes immediately to the medical centre in Bratunac where Oficir is having his wounds dressed. Mr. Petrovic testified that it was only sometime after his return to Belgrade that rumours surfaced about prisoners that had been held at the stadium in Bratunac and a school where an unknown number of people had been killed. That concludes my summary, Mr. President. And I do have a number of questions for Mr. Petrovic. If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you may have noticed that I addressed you as Mr. Petrovic during the course of this summary, but I understand that since the last time you testified you have attained a PhD degree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you prefer that I address you as Dr. Petrovic in this context?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's as you wish, sir. Up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your PhD degree is in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did my master's and my PhD at the same school in Paris, France, that is the so-called Grandes École high school, one of the Parisian universities. It's a higher-education institution for social sciences, and I am -- my diploma is at the Department of History and Civilisations and it's a degree in current affairs, history at present. And I focused on the topic of ex-Yugoslavia. It's an area that I know very well, a field that I know very well. And the title is "The Anatomy of an Auto-destruction: The Rise of Milosevic to Power from 1982 to 1992," so it is the first part of his political career until the war in Yugoslavia, until the civil war, actually. So this is the topic of my thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you currently still engaged in journalism?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. From 2003 I'm not a journalist. I'm a researcher and scientist at the Institute for Political Studies in Belgrade, which is a state institute. But I have kept my journalist credentials because I think bad times for journalism are about to come upon us again, so I would like to perhaps jump in and help if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what specifically you do in your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the institute, I'm in charge of a small centre, the Centre for Geopolitical Studies which is called South-East, under quotation marks, and I cover geopolitical subjects. My latest article which was published is called "The Geopolitics of Energy." The book was published last fall. One of the reasons why I have not appeared earlier in court is that on the 17th we had an important meeting focused on geopolitical studies with French experts from the field in Belgrade and therefore I was ready to come here and testify from the 18th onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've mentioned this article on the geopolitics of energy. Can you just give us as briefly as you can what the idea is or what is the thrust of this geopolitical study that you engage in? What does this discipline concern?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just correct you; it is not an article but rather a book. Over the last years I was mainly focused on three subjects: geopolitics of water, which I published; the geopolitics of food; and the latest was geopolitics of energy. As I live in a small country in which very little attention is paid to such subjects, and they are important for the future of all peoples, both great and small, especially the small ones because what they may have is usually taken from them. I'm doing something that the political class in Serbia should pay its attention to because it's important for the future. Specifically the last book, I got inspiration for writing it from the fact that Serbia, for example, has 60 per cent of all its natural resources in Kosovo, and there is no country that could have sustainable development without this energy. And the United Nations and all its documents say that there is no sustainable development without sovereignty over one's own resources, so I think that the explanation is quite simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. And in your book in particular, do you espouse a particular position concerning -- concerning this issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. When you present a lot of data from across the planet, then you reach some conclusions. It is my own conclusion that the planet is entering upon new, dangerous times of raiding natural resources. We already know that energy crises is looming. There would be energy wars. And this is what I talked most about, that there would be energy wars for resources. I think we all know this, and I think I explain this well to the public at large and the political class, that everyone everywhere should consider this. I published the book a bit earlier before the events about Libya in Africa began, because there you have the West and the Chinese and the Russians. Everyone is there because of the resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was more focusing on the particular topic of the book, which I think you've indicated here reflects the natural resources as distributed between Kosovo and Serbia. Did you take any particular position with respect to your exploration of that issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course, sir. One can learn from the examples set by others. I inquired with the experts from the mining faculty in Belgrade that, for example, the coal reserves in Kosovo are 20 billion tonnes. For a small country which has 7 and a half or 8 million people, 8 million together with the Kosovo Albanians, this represents great future. Even though coal is still a dirty technology, everyone still wants it, the Chinese and the Americans. And the American experts have already managed to make this technology purer. It is not as dirty as it used to be. They also managed to develop techniques by which Co2 can be stocked at great depths under the sea or under rocks and so on. Coal is still very in throughout the planet, and when such a small country can be left without such a resource, then the future is not so bright. And this is what I focused on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned during our conversation this morning that you wanted to explain, I think, or expand upon something that's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think if we can get that up in e-court, it may be helpful. It's P1244. And we should go to page 18880, please. All right. We need to go to 18880.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It takes a little bit more time because we don't have e-court page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate it. We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this part of the transcript of your prior testimony, you refer to an individual here who is denoted as a Colonel Brunel. And in particular it indicates that this is an individual who worked for the French intelligence services. Could you, if you would, explain to the Trial Chamber what about this particular answer that you gave that you found inaccurate or less than perfect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the evidence from almost the end of my previous testimony. We had completed almost everything. But it's not "Brunel" but "Bunel," B-u-n-e-l. He is a colonel, a man charged with military intelligence in French army, who was in Bosnia in the mid-1990s. The public at large knows him perhaps because in 1999 he provided Serbs with some documents, the deployment of targets for the bombing in the war that was to break out later on. He was imprisoned after that but obviously all experts believed that the French wanted to make a gesture of traditional friendship between Serbia and France, though these were obviously targets that Serbs were already aware of. He left service, and after the war in Yugoslavia he was a consultant for many governments throughout the world, consultant about military issues. Perhaps he still has a commentary on Radio France International, which is a state-run radio station where he gives his comments. He was obviously not punished, because if he had done something against his country, he wouldn't be allowed to express his comments on a state-run radio station. I tried to find this in my USB, the interview I did with him, and I promised you that I will send it to you as soon as I come back. It's a text in French which was published in March 2005. It was an interview with him. I did two interviews with him, one in 2003 in Paris and the other one on the Internet when I sent him questions by e-mail and he sent me his answers. This second interview was published in a magazine called "Europa" or "Europe" in Belgrade in an issue for March 2006. I could not tell all the details at the time because the trial was already finished, as you can see from the transcript, but he is a man who would be a very credible, top quality witness. And he told me at the time that he happened to be, in early spring 1996, that is to say, several months after the incident in Srebrenica, in Tuzla. There were some British intelligence men as well. I don't remember other nations, but perhaps Germans were there as well. Probably many from the NATO pact. But he mentioned the French and he mentioned the British. At the time, not just 100, but several hundred combatants showed up. He didn't tell me the exact number, but we suppose that when somebody says several hundred then that's between 2- and 900. So if we take the average, then it's around 500 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's refer to in particular in line 19 of this page 18880 of your previous testimony where you refer to a group -- well, it's transcribed as "a group of a hundred or so combatants," right, this is what you're correcting? This interview that you conducted with Colonel Bunel, you said that it was published -- you conducted two interviews and they were both published; is that right? You have to answer --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. One was published in 2003 in the Belgrade daily "Politika Express," which no longer exists, and the other one I mentioned from which I mentioned the details was published in 2006 in the "Europa" magazine in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from the irregularities in the transcript that you've identified, is there anything in this transcript that's not accurate with respect to this issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think we should not waste time. I told you at the beginning that I have an uncorrected version, and I made corrections with Mr. McCloskey at some earlier point. I think there's no need to go back to these corrections. Everything is fine as far as I'm concerned, but I just wish to add something to the story, because last time I couldn't say everything because it was the end and it wasn't an appropriate moment. I didn't know everything about the procedures, so I told the story at a wrong point in time. So I would just add something if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the Americans themselves questioned these Muslim fighters which as Colonel Bunel said had arrived from the area around Srebrenica where there had been fighting several months earlier, which quite confused me, that these men who were fatigued with many wounded should spend so much time in the area where there was fierce fighting a few months earlier. That was quite strange. However, the Americans said that they had come from that area, and no one except the Americans was allowed to question them. And then after the period of questioning, the Americans moved them to an unidentified location. Independently from that, sometime later through some contacts with the Serbs living in the United States, the Serbian diaspora, I tried to mix and match the data, and then it turned out that many of these fighters turned up in the city of Richmond. I tried to find somebody at the time who would finance a journey of a journalist and a cameraman, but I did not find anyone who would fund me. I wanted to spend some time and wait and try to identify these men at some point. Probably many of them figure today on the lists of missing persons. However, to try and find them after such a long time has passed since then, only the American army could do something like that, and it's a not a propitious time for that. However, I think that this is an important detail, as the source are not Serbs but rather a Frenchman who was a military intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that explanation. What I want to move on to is the video footage that you shot while you were in or around Srebrenica, Bratunac, and so on, on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995. First of all, have you had a chance to review that video footage since the last time you testified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. For everyone, not even the people who had a chance to see it, this is rather traumatic, so I tried not to view it. But I have been invited to a panel discussion in Belgrade where these and other issues from the war will be discussed and with a variety of participants, and once again I will be forced not to say no to the public and I will have to discuss this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can take it, though, that you are quite familiar with the footage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is to show you some of this footage and see if you can, in fact, confirm that it's drawn from the video footage that you shot during July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll have to take a look at P991. Great. We are at 2 hours, 22 minutes, 12 seconds. If we can just play that through 2 hours, 23, 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, can you confirm that this is, in fact, the video footage that you shot on 13 July 1995 in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a part of what I shot at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see that during this footage that we've just seen somebody asks you who you're shooting for and you say the police; you saw that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was an answer to one of these soldiers, because usually when you're somewhere at the front you have problems with filming. And they probably saw me close to Borovcanin, and in order to finish with the subject so that he would not ruin what I was shooting, then I said it, but it was half joking, tongue-in-cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall who was the person who asked you this question? Was that a soldier, was that a passerby, or was that one of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, the refugees didn't ask anything. It was one of the shoulders, the locals. If you rewind it, though it's not necessary, you will see that he has no insignia. And while I was filming -- and while he's asking, I'm still filming; I'm not looking at him. This is the first time -- or not the first time, but I saw him the first time when I watched the materials, because I did not know anyone from this area except Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And here we can see a number of buses and lorries, and you can recall what was going on at that time. If you can just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what you observed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the general atmosphere, what can be seen from the footage? Well, as I said last time, one is shocked by the sheer numbers of people. And by analysing the footage here, you can see that these people are very poor. They are mainly peasants. They are village people. And what I filmed here shows that they were very poor, and the temperature was also very high, in summer. There was excitement because of the war situation. On the other hand, I was surprised that there were no many lorries and buses that were waiting at the ready. And just to reminds you for comparisons' sake, less than a month later Serbs were moving towards Bosnia, Serbs from Croatia. There were no buses, no lorries, people who had their own personal cars or tractors and that was all. It was a huge difference in the treatment of these people. After all, considering the circumstances, so maybe within 48 hours they were all transported in the direction of Tuzla. But from a human point of view, if you had been there or anyone else, it was not a pleasant scene. It is quite shocking, the huge number of people in this small area. But I arrived there at the moment when they were already slowly boarding the buses and lorries, and the crowd was diminishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to another section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should put on the record that you stopped at 2:25:12.2 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. It's a very short question with respect to what the witness said, and I wanted to intervene right away and put the question now. So, Witness, on transcript page 19, you said that you were struck by the difference in treatment which was given to Muslims leaving Potocari by the number of buses and trucks and this with respect to the treatment for Serbs who were leaving Croatia. What did you mean by that, please? Treatment by whom? Who was treated -- who was treating them differently? Are you trying to say that some people were put at their disposal various transportation means and the other group did not get any transportation means? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we compare the two situations, in Bosnia the evacuation speed, so the speed with which the evacuation was carried out, was much faster, it was much more humane. There were no aircraft, no tanks to attack these people. Whereas in Croatia, people were attacked by aircraft, by tanks, by various forces. We actually don't even know who -- which forces are those even today. So the treatment by the Serbian forces was much more humane with respect to the other situation. This is why I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. So are you trying to say that, in fact, the Serbs here in Potocari treated the Muslims who were being evacuated better than Croats treated the Serbs who were leaving from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Much, much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to put on the record that the video was not stopped at 2:25, but 2:23:12.2. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was too eager to agree with you last time, and I see that it is now correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, you indicated that you were shocked by what you saw there. And in the footage we can see a number of men on one side and then a number of women on the other side near these buses and trucks, and while you were there did you see these families, these men and women, being split up or separated from one another?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I really didn't. The speed was great. When you're filming, you had to concentrate. And I have to tell you, first of all, that I'm not a cameraman. I was forced because of the circumstances to film, myself, because a cameraman from Studio B, from the TV station in Belgrade, could not come with me. So I'm a lousy cameraman, but it turned out that the footage is extremely important. If we look at the still which we can see on the screen now, there are more people on the left side than on the right side with the soldiers. Several metres away are the drivers of these buses and lorries, but even now I can try but I did not see the people were separated except for one famous footage with the white house, as it is called, which I shot once when I was filming the possessions of these poor people. So I didn't even know that I would film the white house; I just passed by it. That was the only group that I could see in any place that was separated, and this footage created many problems because everyone accused me that I had destroyed many important parts, but it turned out that this most important footage from Kravica and the other one with the white house do exist in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you do recall, in the footage that you shot, shooting sequences on buses; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the lorries. We can see here one lorry between two buses, here, in the still photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the buses that you were able to shoot video footage of, did you see any men being loaded onto those buses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I even have some footage that should follow this, where I'm entering a bus and there are women in there and some very old women. There was one who even remembered King Aleksandar of Yugoslavia. But I did not see men entering buses separately from women. But of course you must bear in mind that I could not see everything. I could not have been at five locations at the same time. But in any case, I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we can scroll a little bit forward in the video footage. I'm not sure how far ahead it is, but I don't think it's far from here. There we are. All right. We are at 2:24:04.0. And maybe we can just play that right from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't see anything on the screen at the moment. Now it's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've stopped at 2 hours, 25 minutes, 40.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the sequence in particular you were referring to with the elderly woman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you the one who is speaking in this video footage who is asking questions about where they're going and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was me. There is only one or two sentences spoken by a different voice which belonged to a soldier who was behind me and who was telling them that everything will be all right. I don't know him. I just know he was a soldier. And you've seen the old woman. She's a bit old. And he [as interpreted] mixed up King Aleksandar who died in 1934, and she said may God give him and Milosevic health, which she probably said because of fear, because Milosevic wasn't really popular. But as you could see, the scope of ages, between 5 months and 90 years. And I left everything. Whatever I recorded, I left all the footage. And here you can see up there this old man in a cart in the middle of it, and there's a Dutch soldier who is driving him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, once again, you didn't actually see any of these men on the buses or trucks that you went into while you were there on the 13th of July, 1995, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 13th of July, 1995, it was 2.00 in the afternoon, maybe half past 2.00, that was the first bus I entered by chance. I didn't even see who was in there. Had there been a bus with only men in there, I would have recorded that just as I recorded the white house. If there was anything of interest, I recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, there's two questions that I wanted to ask you about this, that particular sequence. The first is, you asked one of the women there about the five-month-old child, whether it was a - I think it was a baby boy, can't really tell - but you asked whether the child was a war child, and I want to know why you asked that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was also topic of the discussion the last time. It's a sensitive issue that could be understood in different ways. My reaction was simple. I know of other war situations throughout the world, and what I noticed was the fact that a town that was surrounded, that was covered in media, in detail, there were many stories saying that people are hungry there and then suddenly we could see babies, brand new babies there. Now, it's through my attention, I don't want to go into geopolitics now, maybe 15 or 20 years ago, if you remember, Gaddafi was telling the whole world that the Muslims will win if they have many children --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time I would like to interrupt you. We are dealing with 1995. But I noted that you didn't answer one question of Mr. Vanderpuye. He asked you: Did you see any of these men on the buses or trucks that you went into? That means Mr. Vanderpuye wanted to know if you saw any men in one of these buses you entered. Your answer was: "Had there been a bus with only men in there, I would have recorded that ..." But that was not the answer Mr. Vanderpuye was looking for. Did you see men in this bus you entered? And that's one question. And the other is, How many buses did you enter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that I had entered into only one bus, this bus that we've seen where women and children were and the very old woman, and that was the only bus I entered. Had I entered into any other buses, I would have recorded what was in there, men as well, but this was the only bus that I entered. I was interested in this column of people passing. And I entered that one bus just by chance. Nobody told me which bus to enter. One has to react quickly in order to get good footage so that you can later make a good documentary. I did not see anything else that would have drawn my attention, so to speak, and made me enter a second, third, or fourth bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that you entered one bus, and we saw that part of the video. Did you see any men in this bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember having seen any. I had my camera on my shoulder and shot the whole bus with it, and one could not see a grown man there. There were some boys, but, no, I did not see a grown man, not a single one, there. They were mostly outside where I also took some footage here. You can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second question I was going to ask you about, and I'll get back to the first one in a minute, but the second question was: At one point during this sequence, either you or the person that is with you says that this is the last group. Do you recall seeing that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I only remember -- I only remember it after hearing him say that and seeing the translation. I arrived in the afternoon. I assume by the number of buses and trucks that this was a process that was going on for two days already. You know, 28.000 people, it takes a while to put them on the buses. And that's the number of people who, according to different data, left for Tuzla, so I guess that this is what he was talking about. This is also the reason why I tried to film this quickly, because everything was happening at a high pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter -- it's P1247.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise what we have on the screen here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are segments of a text of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, it indicates 21st July, 1995. Is that the publication date, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was published under the 1st [as interpreted] of July, 1995. It was a magazine published by the publishing house "Politika," so the date is 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We have the date recorded in the transcript as the 1st of July, but it is the 21st; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of the page you can see 21st of July, 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what I'd like to do is: First of all, you can see right at the beginning of the article they talk about "28.000 Muslims of all ages have gathered here in the Dutch base of Potocari," and that refers to the events that you were filming; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's what this article is about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And on page 5 of the English, page 3 of the B/C/S, you can see a reference there to there have been -- that there were approximately 10.000 children among the refugees. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can that be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be in the middle paragraph, middle column, I'm sorry, in the first paragraph of that column.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph reads: "Demographers will surely find interesting the fact that there were approximately 10.000 children among the refugees." You mean the refugees in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then it reads that "and out of that figure around 8.000 are under 3 years old." And then it says, "the war children," that is a quote, "as they say, this is what they really do." And then it says there, it looks like "hkojas." Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Hkoja is a religious title that Muslims have in our parts in former Yugoslavia. This is a teacher of religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so it says: "Their hkojas ... The motherfuckers ... They are completely surrounded, no food at all, they keep complaining, but they go on procreating ... Is that normal? Would you believe that? Now you tell me, what kind of religion is that, Islam. They made one more corps of soldiers right there in the middle of Srebrenica, who will be after us in 15 to 20 years. Just let them stay as far away from us as possible, my friend, the motherfuckers." That's something that you published where you've quoted someone else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago when I asked you why you asked this young woman about her four- or five-month old child, whether it was a -- whether the child was a war baby, you started to give an answer and you talked about Muammar Gaddafi saying that the Muslims would win if they have many children. And is that essentially the thrust of what we see in this particular article about Potocari, or this particular paragraph, I should say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: You see, my task as a journalist who had to do two jobs at once -- in United States you wouldn't see journalists doing that, or here in Holland they wouldn't find themselves in such a situation. I was on my own. I was at the same time creating the text for the newspaper, which is something completely different than a TV footage documentary. I was criticised about this text before, but I believe this is a very good document. I used the method of complete documentarism [as interpreted]. There is nothing in the quotations that I added. And the purpose of that is to get the dynamics after the event. TV is, in that respect, much simpler to achieve the fullness and the speed that you get on TV. I tried to fill in the text with things I saw or heard there, so this is a quotation I found interesting. You must understand this report of mine includes, for instance, wolves from Srebrenica that were, I guess, photographed during the war, during the period when Muslims were encircled. And you can see some images that I also saw in Balbec [phoen], in Ljuban [phoen], in -- near east, messages of the aggressive Islam. That was a situation where you have two religions in a very small area, something historians are familiar with. I made sure - and I don't curse like this - this is a document. When you're watching war footage, or maybe this film "Searching For Private Ryan," they're cursing all the time; that's war. But here, to be honest, I believe this is one of my better texts. I managed to achieve complete documentary feeling. There is no views of mine, and it's not something that would be similar to my comments of recently that I made about Gaddafi. I thought, and I still think, that I managed to give a completely documentary depiction of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Who were you quoting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was one of the people I ran into there in the period of two days. I cannot give you any names. I remember only the name of Ljubisa Borovcanin, but it wasn't him, he was doing something else. At the time, they were organising the evacuation of the people. So it's one the fighters. It was a view that many held. And on the other side, the Muslim side, if you go and ask them, they would give you an equivalent story. This is why this is credible. A Muslim reading this or a Serb reading this would say, yes, this is exactly how it was. The war, the accumulated hatred, the war as the supreme perversion creates such situations. But these situations were happening one after another, and I just had time to record it. I was just -- later on, I just retyped everything into this text from my notebook, and I was writing it as I was filming the events. And you can imagine what -- how hard it was having to do two things at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So this was a generally widely-held view among fighters. And when you say fighters, you mean Serb forces, VRS, MUP forces; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to all fighters that fought in the war. Croats, Serbs, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what you've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to everyone. I hope that this trial will conclude and not according to my will but God's will. And I would like to say hello to Mr. Petrovic. I would also like to add that it was one man who stated something like that and that's what he confirmed. And then he's asked whether all men were saying that, and then in his following answer he said that all sides that were part of the war used the same terminology, words of hatred. So let us not misquote the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give me a reference where Mr. Vanderpuye said that? I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 30, line 1 and onward, Mr. Petrovic was saying that he was trying to record, by using the images and the tones and the text, that he wanted to record the accumulated hatred that appeared on all sides. And he said that he only retyped the text from his notebooks. And then on page 30, line 14, Mr. Vanderpuye asked him, Is this something that all soldiers were saying there? And Mr. Petrovic said that all soldiers in the war were using such terms, Muslims, Croats, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add another comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. Sorry, no. I'm discussing with Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye is recorded to having said: "When you say fighters, you mean Serb forces, VRS, MUP forces; is that what you mean?" Mr. Vanderpuye was just putting a question to clarify the answer. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, I'm referring specifically to this article and specifically to this paragraph in the article which you say you were, to paraphrase it, proud of. And when I talk about this paragraph in particular, you said that you were quoting from a fighter. And that fighter would not have been a Muslim fighter; right? Or a Croat fighter, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was a Serb fighter. But just to clarify, I said that I was proud of my entire report because it has all the elements of a typical documentary report. This you cannot achieve if you give interpretations of people's words. What you have to do is just quote them, and that's why I'm proud of the work I've done here. And the type of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to another part of this article, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I'm terribly sorry, Mr. Vanderpuye, for interrupting once again. Witness, this article that you wrote, and you say that it's one of the best articles that you have ever written, in the first paragraph that we have here on the screen you talk about mothers that are completely sieged, that are -- it's a city that is besieged, these mothers do not have any food but they continue to complain, and at the same time they go on procreating and they're making babies. So in this article one is asking is it normal. We understand that it is not you who say this but you are just basically quoting somebody else. But at the same time we have seen, a bit earlier, when you talked to the ladies who were in that bus, you asked one of these women if her baby is a war baby, a war child. I would like to know if there's a link between what you said there and if you linked that to this article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that, I did not think of now when we are very comfortably sitting in our chairs and we're pondering upon these questions. So the answer that this woman gave me in that bus, she said, yes, of course, yes. Of course it is. She answered, to my question, yes, of course it is, meaning it is a war child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to know, Why did you put that question to that woman? Is it to congratulate her because she did something good or was it because you were completely astounded by her stupidity? Is that what you wanted to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, well, actually now that I hear your question, thinking about it now it's completely different, but when I was there in that bus, I saw the scene through the visor of my camera, so I saw what you see as well. I just started a conversation basically in the bus, but it was a very difficult situation. The situation was tense. It was hard to be there. And I'm absolutely certain that in my shoes you would have also been surprised and astounded, because it's not a place for children, that bus. And the war, was is not a place for children. And all of sudden you're in this bus and you see a whole bunch of children. I did not really think when I put that question to that woman. I would like to tell you, it's not like now when we're talking about it sitting here. I only thought about it later. I also thought about it later, about it precisely. I thought about your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: But, in fact, you were surprised, if I understand correctly, to see that there were births in that community during that war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, because the situation was really extreme. I was surprised to see so many births. You know, you're besieged for almost 3 years, 2 and a half years -- 3 years, well, from 1192 to 1995 basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would just like to put one last question in order to not take too much time from the Prosecutor. So I would like to know the following: So this surprise of yours in the end, was it because you wanted to congratulate this woman or were you kind of blaming her for what -- for having a child? What is your feeling basically? Are you congratulating her or are you actually blaming her for having a child during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, all children are beautiful, and this child is extraordinarily beautiful. I have to say I really didn't think of that. But before I came into the courtroom, just before I came into the building, I obtained some information via the telephone, and the daughter of one of my close friends has just given birth to a down syndrome child, and I was really totally flabbergasted by this news. So, you know, this is how we -- one should consider children. We should not really make or do any harm to any child, whatever the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think we need our break. Before we break, I would like to remind the Prosecution on the procedure with exhibits. On the 22nd of April in this trial, we gave you some guidance, and I would like to quote two sentences. I quote: "Before seeking admission of an exhibit not admitted through the witness during his prior testimony, the parties should consider their relevance to the instant case and whether they are an inseparable and indispensable part of the prior testimony, without which the prior testimony will lose probative value or will become incomprehensible." Just to remind you, if you are tendering certain documents not admitted through this witness in the previous case, you should put it to the witness and give us some showing. We must have our first break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Petrovic, I have up in e-court some footage from material that you shot on 14 July 1995. I'd like to play this through to counter number 2 hours, 54 minutes, 22 seconds. Actually, before we play it, can you see this on the screen in front of you? Can you see the footage on the screen in front you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell, from the frame that's on the screen, now where this is? If you can't, just let me know. We'll play it and maybe that will help to orient you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think this is the Bratunac-Srebrenica road. It's a few kilometres' distance. You can see refugees here. Actually, I would say that these were Serbs returning to Srebrenica who were just beginning to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play it forward from here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just stopped the film now at 2:55:13.1. Do you recognise what we've seen so far?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us what we've seen. Which direction are you heading and who are the people that we see on these horses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that we are filming in one direction. We just passed the DutchBat, which was between Bratunac and Srebrenica itself. And then the footage stops here at the entrance close to Srebrenica. You can see the top part of a building; you could see people returning, these are Serbs; and parts of Serbian units on horses. These were people who were up in positions above Srebrenica. It's a mountainous area. That's what we saw in this footage. This is the 14th in the morning. I don't know what time it was. Perhaps on some of the raw footage you can see what time it was. I kept during the counter on and off because I wasn't really skilled in that. In front of us we could see the police inspection that was in Srebrenica. They were actually setting up the police authority in the town itself, and that was the reason why we set off behind them. And it was a way for me to actually enter Srebrenica, because it was still not possible to enter just like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All right. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just now, page 35, lines 23 to 25, in answer to Mr. Vanderpuye's question, you've said: "You can see refugees here. Actually, I would say that these were Serbs returning to Srebrenica who were just beginning to return to their homes." My question is: Where were they returning from and in what circumstances did they leave their homes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 when the conflict between Serbs and Muslims around Srebrenica began, it began with a deputy, a Serb, being killed at the entrance to Srebrenica. Then the -- there was a conflict between the populations and then the Serbs left. I think before the war the Muslims were in a majority, but just like many communities in Bosnia, this was a multi-ethnic community. Serbs went to different places in Bosnia, some went to Serbia. They withdrew. So on that day, on the road, these could only have been people who were returning to their homes. In a report later, I interviewed some of those people in those abandoned apartments. I filmed some Muslim abandoned apartments as well. It was a mixed community. And since the Muslims had come down in an organised manner to the DutchBat, this could not have been Muslims at this point in the day. This could only have been Serbs who were coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to state for the record that the footage that we have now up on the screen can be found in the raw footage provided by the witness which is P1349. The start point -- I should, rather, say that the point in the bend of the road where we see the people on horses on this exhibit is at 2:54:46.50 and the corresponding start time in the raw footage video is 00:25.40. And I think I wanted to play further from this point onwards 02 hours, 55 minutes, 13.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you just said it is P1349. This is not listed in your list of documents. I just want to make sure that this is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have it listed, Mr. President, as an exhibit, an associated exhibit with this witness's testimony, but I understand it is already in evidence anyway, and I'm only stating it for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we can, with the Court's leave, continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've stopped now at 2 hours, 55 minutes, 57.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to repeat the conversation that we could see in the subtitling of this section, but I wanted to clarify a couple of things with you, Dr. Petrovic. You were in the car at this point with Ljubisa Borovcanin; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this conversation where you refer to prefabricated mosques or prefabricated mosque being set up on Igman Mountain, who is making that statement; is that you or is that Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On Igman? I don't remember the word Igman being mentioned. Igman is quite a distance from there. It was probably some other word. Igman is close to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's a mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, we see that in the subtitling, so it's a question of whether or not you heard it, I suppose. Are you saying that you didn't hear it, or you didn't see it in the subtitle, the reference to Igman Mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it just now. Perhaps if you replayed it. I'm not sure. I mean, I'm not sure that it's possible that it was Igman that was referred to. It could be an error. There's no context for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe we can back up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll have to go to 2:55:50.94. So maybe 51. 2:55:51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It this can't be correct because we saw another segment. Yes, now you got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, we can try it from here. I think that's close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not close enough. We have to go back a little bit. Apologies. Okay. I think we can start here. First you can see here a reference to a prefabricated mosque. We're at 2:55 -- 2 hours, 55 minutes, 18.9 seconds. Let's try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell who's talking in that sequence? We've stopped now at 2 hours, 55 minutes, 32.4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were three of us in the car and that Borovcanin was there, the driver, and myself. I saw the translation here "Igman." I didn't hear the word Igman, though. I don't know what the context is. Igman is absolutely not in the context, that I guarantee that there is no place for the word Igman here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I heard just at the beginning of that part --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the first word we heard was Igman. Could you replay it again, please, but go a little bit back so that we can hear the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. We are at 2 hours, 55 minutes, 10.4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see that you've -- I think you've heard --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it now. It's either Borovcanin or his driver. I can't tell the voices apart. They say that's how they made prefabricated mosque on Igman like that. And he saw it somewhere else at the front, so that would be the most probable explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here you can see a reference first to a mosque, and then it says "in two more days and this," and then it says "demolished." Can you explain what that's about? Is that a reference to the mosque or is that a reference to something else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot interpret for you from this what exactly it's about. And in any event I would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to a very important detail. This is raw footage, and actually there's much more of it there, this footage being shown to the Tribunal, than is featured in what I actually broadcast. And this is not something that happens in the footage by Christiane Amanpour or something else. Had there been anything important in this raw footage, it would have appeared in the final version. There's nothing much relevant here, generally, that has to do with the Srebrenica story, so we're just chatting along these 3 or 4 kilometres while we're riding to Srebrenica. There's absolutely nothing relevant, that I consider to be relevant, for the Srebrenica story. From a television point of view, this footage is not very good. There's nothing of documentary value here. When you're recording during war time at the front, sometimes if you are riding with somebody you would like to provoke them so you take part in a friendly conversation with them in order to achieve a certain objective. You could do a few things with that. But here, there is a dialogue, there are a lot of F words. In my opinion, it does not have any importance in relation to the footage that I recorded later probably, from the professional point of view. In any case, I'm the only one during the past 20 years who provided their own raw footage, even to my own detriment. This kind of raw footage is something that you will not really get from any journalist who makes such footage. I am probably the only one who actually did hand over this kind of raw footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: And I have no secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer. But, of course, you can understand and appreciate that seeing as you're here in court and this is footage that's before the Court, that even if it may not have documentary value as a television piece, it may have a forensic value for the purposes of this trial. And so the question I asked you was, the reference here in this text to destroying or demolishing, I should say, something, is that a reference to the mosque that was immediately -- that was discussed immediately prior to this -- prior to this remark? Or is it a reference to something else? And since you were there, I figure you might be in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recall, this part of the footage is not in Srebrenica yet. I don't remember seeing any mosques. There were no mosques. The mosque was in the centre of Srebrenica. We were between Bratunac and the entrance to Srebrenica in this part of the footage, so I don't remember what "demolished in two days" in this translation would mean. At that point in time, I think I could not have been able to - and I'm reconstructing it now post festum - I was not able to see the mosque. There is no mosque between Bratunac and the entrance to Srebrenica, as far as I can remember. Perhaps there is one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue playing from 2 hours, 55 minutes, 36.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here you see a reference in the text to "some Arabic thing is already starting here, do you get it." And the answer is "yes, yes ." What's that about? What Arabic thing are they talking about or are you collectively talking about in that vehicle? By the way, we stopped at 2 hours, 55 minutes, 45.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Most probably from this perspective, from 2011, I perhaps saw some detail on the walls of the houses. It was above the door. I think I saw that several times, and in the report there is such a recording. It's what I mentioned earlier. In Balbec, for kilometres of walls of the town there were combat Islamistic messages on the walls. It was held by the Shiites, by the way. But anyway, these were Islam-themed messages, so perhaps it's something that we saw as we were driving past, a word in Arabic. So I think that this was in that context. It wasn't specified, but you have to take what I'm saying perhaps in a relative way. But I think this is the closest explanation to -- for that. There was nothing else. There were no fighters, but there was depiction. There were no fighters from that part of the world, but that -- there was that kind of representation of the fighting and there was that kind of culture present.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue playing from 2 hours, 55 minutes, 45.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here you can see a number of references. One is "as if all this wasn't part of Europe." What's that about in the context of the Arabic thing that was already started that was referred to immediately previously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Most probably it's an additional comment to another civilisation being present in that war. From the beginning of the war we had seen thousands of these Afghan alumni who were fighting in that war on the side of the army of Alija Izetbegovic, and so this is probably something that one of these fighters depicted. I don't believe that anybody from the local population would do that. So it's just a private reaction based on what I knew from other wars, from different situations, regarding the presence of Islamist forces. For example, in 1993, on the 29th of August, I have a photograph in a book of a person who is roasted on a spit from the village of Podravanje, from that same Srebrenica area, this was done from the Mujahedin who had come from the outside. The bulk of them had come from Arabic countries, some from Afghanistan, but mostly they were people who had experience of waging war in Afghanistan and they had brought in this medieval custom. Can you imagine seeing a man roasted on a spit which I had shown on this photograph? So perhaps this was some kind of private reaction. And you can see that this was not footage that was in the final report. I eliminated that as something silly. I mean, can you imagine putting something like this in a report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the reference to the statement that "they've probably brought to us some kind of a plague," is that part of the same diatribe you were discussing that was going on in the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to clarify, as a scientist, I draw a sharp distinction between Islam and Islamism. This absolutely refers to Islamism, which is the bin Laden option, in any case. He was in Sarajevo, his units were there, he had visited Alija Izetbegovic's office. This is documented. And he was helping in the army of Alija Izetbegovic based on this Islamist concept of destroying everything that is Christian, Jewish. I have a book - I know what I'm talking about - the name of my book is "Al-Qaeda, The Green Common Term Against the Judeo-Christian Civilisation" [phoen]. So they were in that area. And you have to understand that perhaps I had rushed out with this sentence amongst soldiers, but I know very well what I'm talking about. We're talking about Islamism, which, in any case, if you're asking me, if I may put it this way: French television filmed them at a check-point near Igman where the Mujahedin are drinking coffee in the morning with French and Dutch soldiers, for example, they were helping them, therefore, at that time, that Christian Europe. And I am a part of that Christian Europe, after all. But I have friends, Arabs, Muslims, from the whole world. I always had them and always will have such friends, so let's make that quite clear. I don't want anything being ascribed to me that is not there. So I am talking about the Islamist option, about bin Laden, who was a hero of the Arab-Muslim world. He is their Che Guevara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please help me to understand the beginning of your answer. You said something about the bin Laden option. Then you added: "He was in Sarajevo, his units were there. He had visited Alija Izetbegovic's office." To whom are you referring in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refer to Osama bin Laden, who was recently liquidated, leader of the Islamist option of Islam whom Renata Vlotau [phoen], your countrywoman who was a reporter from Stern [phoen], from the war in Yugoslavia, saw on two consecutive days visiting Alija Izetbegovic. And his unit of most seasoned fighters, which is called El Mujahid, was in Bosnia throughout the war, and probably some of its members were the ones who roasted men on the spit in the area around Srebrenica. Just so that this is known because this is never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to stop you here. That was not my question. I just wanted to know if you are really referring to the person Osama bin Laden. Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of times, Dr. Petrovic, that this particular segment is not in the Studio B footage. That's the production piece that -- that you produced in -- when you went back to Belgrade in mid-July 1995. I'd like to show you a segment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. First a question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Actually, this question is for Mr. Vanderpuye. And I'm seeking a clarification between the footage of Studio B and the raw footage; what is the relationship between the two? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll put that to the witness. I think the witness can probably tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you've understood Her Honour's question, can you tell us what the difference is between the Studio B footage and the raw footage that you provided to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking generally about the raw footage or materials which are very poor professional quality, as I already said here four years ago. Most of my footage could not be accepted, professionally speaking, at professional TV stations because they are not in accordance with the standards applied today in the world.
