But as I was one of the few people who were present there at the time, that was the reason why some of the segments which were poor in quality were broadcast because of their documentary value. And the raw materials, as Mr. Vanderpuye might help me, is one and a half hours long, or perhaps even more, but more than one hour, and the show was 28 minutes and 30 seconds or so. So here I made a professional mistake, because I'm not a cameraman. I have to keep repeating this. I am what is called a special reporter. So I did not do this part of the work well, in terms of the quality of the footage, because BBC or any other TV station in the world would not allow this to be broadcast, but they would some segments if they didn't have anything else. This is what happened with us from Studio B. So it was at least 1:3 what was discarded and what was broadcast. I think one-third was broadcast or even less than that, but that's more or less the ratio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So in other words, this Studio B footage is an edited version of the raw footage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Judge. We simply entered the editing room and then we watched together to see what satisfied the professional criteria, and we saw very often that the footage is very poor, because the pixels are smaller than they should be. But we took out what could be used and what was important for depicting the general atmosphere of this historic event as it turned out to be later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just about to play the Studio B segment of roughly this footage. I think it is actually the same start point. As you recall in the footage we played earlier - and that should be at counter 2 hours, 55 minutes, 7.4 seconds - you will see this gentleman in a -- on a horse who the occupants of the car talk to or he salutes the occupants of the car. You'll find this same footage just now in the Studio B footage that I'm just going to play you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go first to 2 hours, 55 minutes, 57.69 seconds, we should see it here. That's just the heading so we know where we are. Okay. And following this we'll go so 2 hours, 56 minutes, 7.05 seconds. And I think we can play it forward from here. You'll recognise this footage as we saw previously in the raw material. We can play it from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this, Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We are at 2 hours, 56 minutes, 7.6 seconds. This is the trial video, and we have now the Studio B segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can stop it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you may have noticed, Dr. Petrovic, on this particular footage it is interrupted by what we see and what this Trial Chamber has learned is the footage from the Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July. Now, I know that you've been asked about this before, but other than what you've already said about this edit in the Studio B footage, do you have any explanation for why it is, first of all, that this 13 July footage appears in the middle of a 14 July sequence on the Studio B footage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it sounds unbelievable, but the explanation is very simple. Let me first explain something else. As you can see, there is very little of what was the conversation in the car, where the camera is lowered because it's sitting in my lap, with the four-letter words being said. This is the footage shot as we were driving along, so that one could see that it was filmed on the move. And as many parts could not be selected as part of the reportage, I simply cannot remember so many years later, but one of the two editors who were working in turn probably contributed to including this part which was filmed also from the car. And when the show was broadcast, I was not aware what would happen with this, that these were the dead and so on. Or perhaps I was aware. But the only professional reason why we included it there is because it's shot on the move. It's not still, but it was shot from the car. That was the only reason. We had a problem. 28 and a half minutes is a lot of time, and there should be a lot of footage that needs to satisfy the standards. And I haven't satisfied them because I'm a poor cameraman. Perhaps I was shooting something two or three times in my life. But I had a problem because everything had to be done quickly, it needed to be edited in two or three days, and we didn't have enough footage. Especially when the story begins, you cannot just stop footage. If you have a footage which is filmed on the move, then you have to have certain length covering the period that I spent on the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica. And, yes, this is footage from quite a different location. It's from the location on the road Bratunac-Tuzla, in the direction of Kravica, that is to say. But the only reason was technical. And I was not the only one who had an impact on this but also the technician, that is to say, the editor, who was working on this because of the shortage of footage that was good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the Court, for the record, this Studio B footage is P1250. It's V0003826. The footage sequence that we're talking about, where we began here in the trial video, is found in P1250 at 0 hours, 17 minutes, and 5 seconds. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to the witness. We heard voices of the people in the car. Who were in the car talking, did you recognise the voices? I refer you to the last part of the footage we saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you mean the part when the soldier on horseback comes along and asks us how we are, yes, but there are three persons in the car from Bratunac to Srebrenica. I am one, Commander Borovcanin is the other person, and there's the driver as well. So it can only be the voices of the three of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who was talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recognise my own voice, but in certain moments I'm not sure if it's Borovcanin who is the other person speaking or the driver as well. I think at some moments it was also the driver. I cannot remember the voices because I heard them last time in 1995 during a short period. So I think you can understand that when it comes to the tone of voice, particularly of this third person, if I were to meet this person here, now, I wouldn't know that it was the same person, if I were to judge just by the voice. But there were three of us in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you don't recognise your own voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I mostly do recognise it when it's louder. I mostly recognise. And as for the swear words, it was me who spoke some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, we have a transcript of this video segment. It's our position that we have two voices on this transcript, notwithstanding what the witness says, that's just our position. What I'd like to show the witness is you indicated -- if we can just back up for a moment to 2 hours, 56 minutes, 7.05 seconds and see the beginning of this footage of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have this footage that you've described that you shot as you drove past the warehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have to answer for the record, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was on the 13th of July in the afternoon in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this was after you returned from further down the road in the Konjevic Polje direction towards Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Because the car was going along the side where I was sitting on the right-hand side, and the right-hand side can, as far as it seems to me from this perspective, can only be the one leading towards Bratunac. Perhaps I'm wrong, but that's how it seems to me. After all, this is two or three seconds, maybe not even as much, this particular footage. Because I was filming that, don't forget that, while the Muslims were shooting at the car, and everywhere around, not just at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you can hear some shooting right at the beginning of this clip; isn't that right? You hear some loud shooting or explosion or some noise to that effect; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's right, because close to this place and close to the road is a stream almost without water and the Muslim forces were on the other side. I have explained that but I can repeat it again what was the situation in which I was filming this. There were Muslims who were surrendering themselves, there were Muslims who were shooting at the Serb, there were Muslims who were shooting at the Muslims who were surrendering themselves. So you can imagine the situation in which I shot this, and thanks to that, you have this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's took a look at another section. Here we have this same footage slowed down. And it's at 2 hours, 56 minutes, 23.06 seconds. Hopefully I've got it right. Okay. We're at 2 hours, 56 minutes, 23 seconds, and we can play it from here. It should be a slowed-down version of the footage we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this footage you can see at least three soldiers, one at the beginning of the clip, another one we see walking by, and this one, the last one in this clip, standing in front of a bus with his thumbs up in the air. Is it your position that at the time that you're shooting this footage that the shooting that we can hear is coming from the Muslim side in your direction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. As for the slow-motion footage, I never had a chance to see it in Studio B. It was the first time that Mr. McCloskey's office told me that you had technical abilities to do that. There were three trucks and one bus with doors open back and front. You can count them. There were -- you can count these soldiers and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Soldiers rather than trucks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- three soldiers. I know that they were shooting at us all the time along this stretch. I later on when I returned to Belgrade was that I became scared. This is how I always reacted during the war operations. I did not think about that at the time, but when I think about it now I can tell you that I would never film such scenes as these again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The reason why I asked the question is that none of these three soldiers we can see in the footage appear to be taking cover or trying to get out of the way or ducking behind objects or anything to avoid getting shot if they're being shot at from the Muslim side. Can you explain how you reached the conclusion that you were being shot at from the Muslim side, where you can see the behaviour of these soldiers is someone incongruous with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not asked this question during my previous testimony, but if you have a look at the hangar which was discussed in detail here at court, they were covered, and so was our car at the moment, just that one piece of ground, because beyond that, beyond the hangar, was the stream and the area where the shooting was taking place, so here they are covered by the building, which explains why no one is holding a rifle in a combat position. They are completely covered by the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just back up a couple of frames.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now we have -- I'm sorry, we're at 2 hours, 56 minutes, 33.4 seconds. Now we have the footage of the warehouse, and you see the bodies that are in front of it. You've testified to that before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated, when I spoke to you had this morning, that you had received certain information with respect to the doors that we can see here in this footage; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey is here as well. I think that at the Popovic et al. trial there was a big change towards the end because it was established that the hangar had its door closed, and this can be seen thanks to my footage. I just ask how is it possible if that happened that many witnesses who testified in this case, dozens and dozens of them, said that it was open and they saw up to 1500 dead. That was the highest number. 500 or 1000 or 1500, and this was judged to be 15 to 20 dead men shot during the few seconds as the car was passing by, and it's strange that no one was taken to account for such lies, because here you can see in this footage that the door was closed, and there is no footage anywhere else as far as I know showing the door open which, in my view, is a very significant detail in this case, speaking as a layman, because I'm not a professional in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Is this something that you're testifying to from memory of having recalled seeing it, or is this based on some information you learned since you last testified, that is, the conclusion concerning the doors that we see here in the clip?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during my testimony, this was not mentioned at all. It was later on that I learned, because I wanted to learn what happened with Mr. Borovcanin and so on. So in the meantime, during these years, somebody told me that. I cannot tell you who, but obviously I never paid any attention to this detail, for example, because this is just two second, and it can be seen quite clearly here that the door is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that the people that we see piled up in front of this warehouse were judged to be, I think you said 15 to 20 people. And when you say "were judged to be 15 to 20 people," to whom are you referring? Are you referring to your own estimate or is that the estimate of some person or authority other than you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is an absolutely amateur estimate, but when we look at the space how wide the door is and the area to left, I haven't heard any expert opinion on that subject. I would like to hear it, but I have not. This is my own estimate. Considering the area which was filmed and how many people there are, this is how I reached the number of 15 to 20. It's like, though this is a very unpleasant scene, of course, and I don't like to see it frequently, but it's like on stadiums throughout the world people count how many football fans can be in one square metre, so this is similar to that. It's a sort of physical measurement and an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see the slow motion part again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we started out at 2 minutes -- 2:56:23. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the witness to focus on the whole part, the slow motion, and then I would like to ask you after that about your estimation how many bodies were there that we see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We stop at 2:56:44.7 seconds. Now you have seen the whole sequence. Explain your estimation again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If possible, I would like to hear from everyone present what their estimate is, but once again, I think that it could not be more than 20 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just please have in mind that these are 2 or at most 3 seconds which I did not expect to film. First of all, I was in a car which was occasionally being shot at from that site, from beyond the hangar. So it's not the same as when I was filming it. We are relaxed now. But at the time, I could not think about everything. You know, when someone's shooting at you, I don't know if anyone ever shot at you, but it's quite a fearful feeling that you have. So this is my estimate post festum when I'm watching the footage now. I did not hold it to be very important because I filmed many other things as well, but really, frankly speaking, I would say that it is about 20 people. Because I remember that earlier on at the beginning the American state secretary had some footage from the satellite when people were boarded on buses. There was something like that at the beginning. And then estimates were made how many people could have been on -- in this field which I also filmed, and the estimate was that it would be enough to fill one bus. I'm not an expert for such issues. It's just the visual feeling that I have, so please take it as a post festum estimate, because at the moment I did not register it at all. I didn't know for a long time that there were three soldiers depicted in the footage because it all passes along very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall how many doors this building, Kravica warehouse, had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the moment I was not aware of the totality of the footage, what we can see now and what we saw at this other trial four years ago. I really cannot tell you. But if one could ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to stop you. I'm asking about your recollection. How many doors did this building have at that time? I'm not talking about the footage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure, actually, that we have all -- this is all of the footage. Maybe we can just play it out just to be sure, but I think it's pretty close if it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. We stopped now at 2 hours, 56 minutes, 52.4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, when you shot this video footage, did you at any point stop the car that you were in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My answer will be brief. I really do not remember stopping or else I would have taken some footage had we stopped, because at the time the fighting was still going on, this is not -- the 11th of July was not the last day of the fighting. There was fighting also on the 13th. I could hear shots throughout the day -- throughout the afternoon, rather, not throughout the day. Once I left the compound and headed down the road, there was shooting all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated in your prior testimony that Mr. Borovcanin with whom you were at the time took one of his men or went with one of his men to the hospital or the Bratunac Health Centre. Do you remember that? You have to answer, if you have the translation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did that occur? Was that in the vicinity of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, it was a different location. I cannot tell you at this point whether that was towards Bratunac, towards the centre of Bratunac, or maybe earlier when the footage of Muslims surrendering were made. We appeared almost immediately after the events and we heard that Borovcanin's officer had been wounded. And then we immediately headed on, and during that stretch we filmed the Kravica warehouse. As far as I can remember, it was immediately after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the footage was shot on the way to the Bratunac Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that you didn't go with Mr. Borovcanin to the health centre; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, let me be precise. I was with him in the car on the way to the health centre, but I did not enter the health centre. I remained outside of the building, and they brought him in for treatment. I certainly didn't think -- see any of the premises of the health centre inside. There was no reason for me to enter the building. I was waiting outside, I think, next to the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the person who was injured, Oficir, did he get in the car with you and Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We are arriving and then I think the meadow was in Sandici where the Muslim soldiers who had surrendered were located and that's where it happened. Before I started shooting them as they were surrendering, I mean, filming them as they were surrendering, and then Borovcanin immediately decided what to do. Immediately after I finished my filming, and that was only a few minutes after that, he decided to take the guy to the health centre. I think he had a Motorola, the walkie-talkie, and someone must have informed him about it. But we passed there immediately after the shooting itself. I wasn't an eye-witness, but Borovcanin also wasn't an eye-witness to the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You received some information concerning the injury that was suffered by one of Borovcanin's men; right? That's what you wrote about in your article and I think you testified about it also in 2007.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the information that you received about the injury to Borovcanin's men was before you proceeded to the health centre; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably it was within a few minutes. I heard it and then along the way maybe I wrote it down. You will understand that I don't remember details. But it was there at that location that we received the information. I heard them talking between themselves about it and I wrote that down because it was an interesting documentary-type detail in a war-time situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What did you hear them talking about, just the injury to Oficir? The fact that some Muslim was trying to get out from the building, as you've testified to before, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I must say that I haven't checked my text, the one you're referring to, in a long time, but there was no one entering any buildings. These are rather big buildings. This was all happening next to the buildings. We're all excited. The soldiers were also in a heightened state after the event because this Muslim fighter bravely jumped, took the gun, and started shooting. I only heard about that, but I did hear about it at the place where the event took place. One of the soldiers that were there said that such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you some other footage, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you should be aware of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am. Thank you, Mr. President, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P1346, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't see the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are just finding the exact point in the counter. And we found it. Thanks, Ms. Stewart. It's 16 minutes, 43.7 seconds. I think we can play it forward from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see this -- do you recognise the road that you are on at this point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're in the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which direction are you going?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since the mountains are on the right-hand side, we are heading towards Drina, towards Serbia, and on the left-hand side is the road Bratunac-Tuzla, from Bratunac to Tuzla, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you're heading in the direction of Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's keep playing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who is in the car with you, by the way? Borovcanin is in the car with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Last time I could not remember whether he was there. I mean, his driver, whether he was there on the first day. But since I'm sitting in the front and we can see the walkie-talkie, the Motorola, I'd said that Borovcanin is driving. Now, whether his driver was in the car or not, I'm not sure. I cannot remember. It wasn't important for me. I was making a report. I wasn't interested in who was with Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right before you we play it, you hear he says "Oficir, Bor"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That was a code-name. Oficir is officer and Bor is pine. This shows that he's not addressing an officer but they are using the code-name when they are talking over the communication set. Maybe -- General Tolimir is an officer, maybe he can explain these things better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: And he then says "stop the traffic after you." And that's what I was saying earlier, that the convoys had to stop occasionally because of the fighting on some stretches of the road, the same road where we were. That's what you can see in the following sentence, "stop the traffic behind you."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you can see here we have a reference "LJB," that would be Ljubisa Borovcanin, who's speaking, who says "Oficir, Bor"; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, Oficir is a person and Bor is the speaker, as in Borovcanin; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Possible. I didn't think about it that way, but it's possible. This is a military issue. I wasn't really paying that much attention to their conversation. I was more following what's recorded, the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that. You wrote in your article, though, that Oficir was one of the -- I've forgotten the term you used, but it was a flattering comment in relation to his position in Borovcanin's unit, that Borovcanin was his commander; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that it's a nickname. Officers, soldiers often have nicknames. You can verify that elsewhere, but I think it was a nickname. I don't think he was actually an officer either of the army or the police. It was most probably his nickname. But I cannot say that with any degree of certainty. You would need an expert for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it might be a translation issue, but I would just point you to your article. I think it was P1427 - there's the dyslexia - 1247. And in particular you say, at page 5 of the article -- and we don't need to -- I'll just read it. We don't need to put it up because we've seen it already, but you say, in recounting the story --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- about how Oficir was injured. You say that he is one of Ljubisa's Special Forces members; right? And you say Oficir is one of the hopes of Borovcanin's formations, so the commander goes immediately to the medical centre in Bratunac where Oficir, in quotes, Oficir - not officer - is having his wounds dressed; right? In this footage you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should wait for the answer. We would like to hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, as I can see here in the text, Oficir is with -- is in quotation marks and it is, according to me, clear that this is not his function but his nickname. It's been a while and I haven't had an opportunity to read this -- re-read this text. Based on the text I can say that this Oficir was a nickname. I never met the man, but I did hear comments by other soldiers there who said that he was an experienced fighter, a good fighter, and I put that into my text. All countries in the world when they are writing reports about their troops, they always try and say the nice things about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So here you see Ljubisa Borovcanin giving Oficir an order which is to stop the traffic behind you. You can see that on the screen in the text and we can play it through so you can hear it. We are at 17 minutes, 10 seconds -- 10.5 seconds. Maybe we should play this through a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen because now we see the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where we are now on the video? We're at 17 minutes, 34.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are on the same road. I am not sure because while we were editing I was trying to remain in chronological order, but now we see the left side of the road when compared to the footage from a moment ago. So this is the segment of the road where some of the Muslims are surrendering to the Serb army and others are still fighting, and there are a third group of Muslims that are shooting on those Muslims who are surrendering. And there's another clip where we can see people coming down the hill. This is all very surreal, and I did my best with the camera I had. If I had a professional cameraman, this would have been of much better use for you as well, but this camera could not record, film, everything, especially things that were far away. But, yes, this is the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Petrovic, there is evidence in this case that Oficir, whose name is Rade Cuderic, was a member of Mr. Borovcanin's unit; that he was directed to stop the traffic behind him, which was in fact just in front of the Kravica warehouse; and that after this direction, that the executions that occurred at that warehouse began. Can you tell this Trial Chamber if that comports with your recollection of what transpired on that day, that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I hear for the first time in my life this name Cuderic; I think that's the name you mentioned. While I was there on the spot, I did not know any of these things. And you are also assuming that a mere journalist would know what officers are discussing between themselves during military operations. I was certain on previous occasions when I was listening to this footage that this is what they were talking -- what was being talked about. I believe that it was because of the stretches of the road were under fire that they were stopping the traffic with buses and trucks where the women and children were so that they wouldn't be in danger. This is the first time I've heard of this name, Cuderic. I would have put his name in the text if I'd known it, if I'd heard it, but I hadn't, especially since I was toad that he was wounded in the health centre -- I mean, he was wounded and then taken to the health centre. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long after this order that you see Borovcanin give to stop the traffic, approximately, in your best estimation, was it before you were at the Kravica warehouse and shot the footage that we see there? About how long?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's impossible to answer this question that you've put to me. You've seen in the footage that some soldiers were shooting against the hills from where the Muslims are opening fire. So between the conversation over the Motorola and that event, I was focused on filming. I was not embedded like the Americans embed their journalists; I didn't have a flak jacket or anything. I was focussed on my own journalistic madness, and I cannot tell you from this distance how much time has elapsed. I would like to be able to help you, maybe earlier, yes, but unfortunately ... fire -- there was fire coming from everywhere around us. I don't know whether you've been in a war, did you ever witness firing against you, but this question that you're putting to me 16 years after events, it's impossible. I'm sorry if I've disappointed you with giving the answer that I'm giving, but I promised I would speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all we can ask for, Dr. Petrovic. I see that I'm just about out of time. But I want to ask you one last question, and that's again drawn from your article on the 21st of July, 1995. It's P1247. I have it as page 5, so I assume it's page 3 in the B/C/S. And you describe the circumstances under which, as you've said today, you returned in the direction of Bratunac past the Kravica warehouse as concerns Oficir. And the last thing you say in the fourth paragraph on the page in the English is: "The one who killed the policeman died on the spot." This is a policeman that was killed at the warehouse; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't next to the hangar. It was at the location where the Muslims were surrendering. It's a different location. It's along the same road, but it's quite a way away from it. I think it's called Sandici. I didn't know the name of the place for quite a while, but these are two different proper names, Kravica and Sandici. The Oficir in quotation marks, that happened in Sandici. That's something I was not eye-witness to but I was told about by the soldiers who were quite excited about it, and I also said that the police forces are carrying out the tasks in the Israeli manner, namely merely as little casualties as possible. These were all trained policemen who were policemen even before the war. Serious people, maybe one of the best units that the Serbs had during the war. They were better soldiers than many other soldiers available to any of the warring parties at the time. At least that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say at page 3 of this same article, and it's the last paragraph of the English page. The B/C/S we can find with the heading "A Chance for Krstic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe we have it at page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And there you can see, you say: "On the 5th day of the Serbian offensive, the able-bodied men from Srebrenica attempted to break through across Konjevic Polje and towards Tuzla." If you look at the next couple of sentences past that, you will say: "They were soon in disarray and the last battles with Serbs, on the night of 12 July, they had suffered over 500 deaths," and you say "they also had the misfortune to run into the MUP Special Forces." By that I take it you mean the Special Brigade, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have to go to the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "Borovcanin's unit." And you say: "In addition to Mladic, as on so many previous occasions," you then say "I personally had the chance to see for myself once again that whoever runs into a member of the Special Forces is dead?" And that's what you saw; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard on this location where this person nicknamed Oficir was wounded, and I also saw from a distance some of the fighting along the route. I filmed the anti-armour gun, I saw Muslims coming down from somewhere high up, and one could also hear constant fighting. I may have gone too far with this sentence, but in essence it is correct. The unit never committed any war crimes, at least nobody knows of any. They were disciplined throughout. Many of the units that participated in the civil war in former Yugoslavia had terrible discipline, but this unit was different and that was the reason why I accepted to be Mr. Borovcanin's witness, but I did not see, personally, what is mentioned in this sentence, namely that whoever runs into a member of the Special Forces is dead. I didn't see that for myself. I may have pushed it a bit too hard, but in essence, the comment is correct and it's a consequence of my experience after having heard about this soldier being wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Dr. Petrovic, I'm out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Apologies for exceeding my time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does this conclude your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I left that part out. Yes, it does, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our second break now, and we will resume at 6.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now you may commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again I would like to greet all those present, and I would like this day in the courtroom to end as God wills and not as I will. I would like to greet Dr. Petrovic and wish him a pleasant stay in our environment. In order for both of us to have an easier time of it, I'm going to begin from the end of this examination-in-chief. And then I would just like to ask you: When I put my question, you wait, you watch the letters, the cursor on the screen, when that stops, then you may begin to answer my questions, and I'm going to try to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 68 of today's transcript, you were asked about the sentence that you quoted and that you heard, about who gets in the way of the specials does not live. I'm asking you this: Are you thinking about the enemy in battle, if they happen to come across Special Forces, or did you mean something else? It's important to clarify this for the transcript. I apologise to you, and I thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, thank you as well. And, of course, the sentence perhaps did come out a bit clumsily, but what I meant was their combat glory, according to all international rules of law, they respect the law but are merciless in battle. So I just wrote what was already known about them before and what I saw in some other place, not in Srebrenica but near Semizovac and up at Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. On page 67, line 24 on, you were asked about the article that was published. This is page 2 in the B/C/S. This was something that the Prosecutor quoted from, and he quoted roughly as follows: How 500 Muslims were killed who had tried to break through from Srebrenica and how 500 of them were killed, they had the misfortune to run into the MUP Special Forces. This is what was heard from Borovcanin. I'm paraphrasing. I didn't take it down word by word. You probably remember that question. So my question is this: Did you hear this in Sandici before you went to Kravica to film what you filmed almost accidently, you yourself didn't know what you filmed until later? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you for this question. I think a clarification is called for. Perhaps I made a mistake in the date, but this is subsequent information, so I'm not able to give you precise information. At that time, only one other journalist in the world in 1991 wrote about that. I don't know his name. I think he's Swedish. He wrote one text about it. I talked about it earlier, in earlier years, in Serbia, in different occasions, because this is an event that neither the Serbs nor the international community nor the Muslims ever mentioned. This happened - I'm just not sure about the date; I think it was the 13th or the 13th and the 14th of July - the Muslims, those forces that were fighting against the Serbs, at one point were concentrated and they attempted a break-through like this in the form of an arrow. They were concentrated along the Tuzla axis because, as far as I can remember, Muslim territory was not that far away, and it was important for them to reach that territory. So they had formed a wedge and had set off on their break-through. I heard this from different people, so in that sense there is a reconstruction of the events that there was an enormous danger of them through this wedge movement of moving and then turning right towards Tuzla. No, no, not Tuzla. This other town on the Drina, towards Zvornik. And just like during the whole war, the Serbs, and you probably know this better than I do - not probably, definitely - the Serbs suffered from certain failure. They had fewer men. And there was a danger of the town falling into the hands of Muslims and that would have been a world attraction. This is not something that Ljubisa Borovcanin told me. I know this for a fact. But I know that I heard this from different people. I asked that and it was confirmed and I was told this by the Swedish man who confirmed this event. So probably had this Special Brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska not been there, the Muslims would have perhaps even reached Zvornik. This is why I took this as an example of a disciplined unit, and they say that several hundred up to about 500 casualties were suffered. This doesn't imply 500 dead, that perhaps would have been too much, but it means dead and killed and wounded. But this was taken to be as a large success of the Serbs and a failure by the Muslims because it's well known that a person who is fighting for their life in war time has an upsurge of strength, and they had gone into this with this extra strength, into this break-through. So a part of the UNPROFOR forces, a part of the international forces, Serb forces, and Muslim forces have not spoken to this about this day. If they made an effort, probably they would have found out more about this, because they told the Swedish journalist about this and all that they had lived through once they had reached Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First, indeed, please wait that the translation has finished. And I would like to ask the witness, Mr. Petrovic, please slow down while you are answering questions. You are talking very fast and it's very difficult for the interpreters and the court recorder to catch everything. Slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, My Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, well, all right, since both of us were fast and we created problems for the interpreters because of the transcript, can you please tell us clearly whether you at this point in this article of yours post festum are writing about the casualties that occurred in combat in the Muslim column that was moving from Srebrenica to Tuzla? So we're talking about events that happened in battle and about events that you heard from this journalist and from others who spoke about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did mention that event. I was inspired by that event because it had drawn a lot of attention because it was something that was tacitly treated by all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Petrovic, are you aware that witnesses here, Muslims, testified how on the road that the column was moving along they saw over 300 dead who had been killed in clashes, in fighting, because of the minefields that they had encountered? Did you hear information to this effect from others? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I missed that detail. I don't remember reading about that detail or hearing about it in the context of these trials. Unfortunately, this sentence was not mentioned when I testified before the Tribunal in a case here four years ago. I'm sorry, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. You were asked a number of times here during the cross -- the examination-in-chief about events that occurred 16 years ago. Of course, the events that I'm asking you about also occurred 16 years ago and it's difficult to give precise answers to all the questions that are being put to you. So please, you were asked here how you got information that the doors on the hangar in Kravica were closed. Since there were several questions during the examination-in-chief, this was on page 67, line 21, where you were asked to describe this, are you able to say now how you got this information, and did you see this later in the film? Or how did you see that the doors were closed? Are you able to tell us what your recollection of that is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, my information comes from stories that were told to me indirectly by other people in Belgrade after the events occurred. I recall being told that Mr. McCloskey's team had to do a part of the job over from the beginning and that this was a detail that the Defence of Ljubisa Borovcanin pulled out at the last minute in the trial. I didn't really deal with the particulars of all of that. I think that is actually the body of the information. No one from The Hague told me this. This is something that I heard in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. A little bit earlier I had stressed that even the Muslims say that there were 300.000 dead?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the road from Srebrenica. So can we now look at D151 page 2 so that we can see that I'm not just talking off the top of my head but that I have testimony about that. Can I ask e-court please to show D151 page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, this document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not recorded. It is under seal and in that case it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, I'm kindly asking you to read this to yourself. Please do not read anything from this statement aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are showing the first page so that we can see that this is a statement by a witness. Can we look at paragraph 3, which states: "As we made our way through in the direction in which the first group had gone, we came across warnings or, rather, signs saying 'mined.' I assume that our people who had passed earlier through these areas left these signs. From there we headed towards Pobudska Kamenica, where we met up with a part of the first group, but the Chetniks surrounded us there and opened fire on us, killing over 300 people and wounding a large number." I did not ask you this earlier when we were on this topic, but is this what you meant, losses in combat, when you were talking about the 500 casualties that we referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, most probably yes, it does coincide with the story that I reconstructed from that time-period. I don't believe that there were any other significant events. In my opinion, perhaps the military historians would need to explain why this was just passed over without being talked about, because it's a quite powerful clash of the two sides, and this is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Today or tomorrow we are going to show you the chronology of the events from that break-through. I'm just giving you this information because at this place that we are talking about, many witnesses say that there was a much higher number of casualties. This information comes from witness testimony. My question about this now is -- actually, when you look at the document on the chronology, then we can talk about how many dead there were in the corridor, and you will be able to see what the Muslims themselves say about the casualties they inflicted on the Serbs and how successful they were in the break-through that you were talking about. But my question now is this: Did you hear that at the time Muslim artillery fired at Zvornik, which is what you mentioned earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the information I have is that they were perhaps the closest to the Zvornik-Kula spot. I don't know which weapons they were firing from; I'm not able to say that here. But they were already close to the Zvornik-Kula area. And for those present, that is outside of Zvornik in the direction of Sarajevo. It's an ancient fortress, the remains of an old fortress, and that spot was very important to all parties in the war. I don't know if they fired at the town itself, but I know that they were very close to breaking through and to turning to the right towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. As a journalist, did you hear at the time that that Muslim column was moving from Srebrenica towards Nezuk and Tuzla via the positions of the Zvornik Brigade, the so-called Baljkovica area that is on that route? Did you hear anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I don't remember the Baljkovica toponym, but in any case you could see in my footage a degree of that area. It's a mountainous area, it's summer, the area is forested, it's a very unfavourable terrain for battling, and it's logical that they took those hills to move towards the Tuzla area. But I did not encounter Baljkovica as a toponym at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Please, we'll move on to what you filmed or what you saw. As I indicated earlier on page 67, 21, you talked about footage which registered in front of the door of the hangar in Kravica a certain number of bodies, and you estimated that the number was roughly around 20 bodies. You were asked several questions in relation to that. Can you please tell us whether these were all the bodies which you filmed at the location in Kravica or is there another footage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, all bodies which I personally saw were filmed. But let me repeat once again, my footage hardly lasts 3 seconds. It's maximum 3 seconds while passing by Kravica. I shot maybe another 3 or 4 dead people in Srebrenica itself on the 14th of July, the following day, as compared to Kravica, and that was in the centre of the town of Srebrenica, and these were dead Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I had in mind, Dr. Petrovic. So what is registered in the footage and then only later you said, during the examination-in-chief, that you discerned what was included in the footage. I have not emphasised that in my question. Can you please tell me whether I'm right or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 67, you talked about the place called Sandici where you also saw one dead person in Sandici. And you talked about the incident that you heard about later on, you and Mr. Beara [sic] as well. Mr. Borovcanin - I'm sorry - it was a slip of the tongue. Please excuse me. Please tell us, later on, on page 67, you said -- actually, you said on page 57/1 that according to your estimate in the Sandici meadow there was a total of as many people as could fit into one single bus. Can you please clarify this a little bit for us so that we would have a clearer picture of that? Thank you. Because you were asked by cross questions about one and the same subject.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it's the same as with the dead in front of the hangar in Kravica; it's just my personal estimate. Once again, I say that -- perhaps it's not appropriate, but just like during football matches, you keep estimating, also during rallies or demonstrations, how many people are on Trg Republike, the republic square in Belgrade, and the police always say there are much fewer and the protestors say that there are much more and then that's repeated in all countries. So I made the estimate on the basis of my own footage to the effect that the number of people was such that they could all fit into one bus, so perhaps around 100 people or less. Today I think that would be around 100 people. But I saw it in a moment. I was not continually in that place or in any other place. I was in passing everywhere. Sometimes I would spend a little time somewhere, but it was combat zone, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Did you see that at this location in Sandici Mr. Borovcanin stopped the buses with civilians who were transported from Srebrenica to Tuzla in order to board on them those who were underaged and who were not yet old enough for combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this scene is something that is etched on my memory, because the following year in 1996, or perhaps even in 1995 already, I saw one of these boys who were one of the people featured in a British-produced TV show in which he told an unbelievable story to which I was one of the witnesses at that very time. Namely, I saw with my own eyes that the then Colonel Borovcanin, today he's a general, stopped the buses and the lorries - I don't remember anymore, perhaps it was a mix of the two - in order to select at least ten or so boys who were younger than 18, and were obviously not fighters at all, that was on the meadow in Sandici, and he ordered that they be included in the convoy going for Tuzla, and he left for Tuzla with the other children. And I will keep claiming this as long as I live. In his testimony in the BBC TV show, he said the unbelievable thing that he hid behind some water there. Now, if someone was to go there, there's no water and there is no spring. There's no water fountain or anything. Then he said that it was a miracle that he somehow managed to reach Tuzla. It was obviously a spin doctor's job, one of the experts for manipulation, because I saw Mr. Borovcanin - and this is why -- this is one of the details why I testified - I think he is a highly moral man and that he did not allow, once we got there, when he saw these children that they should be kept together with the soldiers, and they all left. This is what I claim. And no one is brought to account for these false testimonies today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P1251 in e-court. Page 56. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether you perhaps recognise anyone from these stills, anyone who was transferred to this bus to go with other women and children from Srebrenica who were being sent to Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General, it is the boy in the lower line in the middle. These are stills from my own report. I do not recognise the others. The man in still A was also selected for a British documentary. I was told that this man had gone missing or had perhaps been killed. These were stories that I heard, but I don't know much about this. But as for the boy, this is the boy who was with other children of the approximate age, boarded onto the bus or lorry going for Tuzla. So he went to Tuzla from that location. This is what I absolutely assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us with which letter is the still marked, the boy whom you see. You said this is the boy, but you didn't say which image it is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I said this is image E. And F is a shot from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, is there perhaps any video footage of the incident in which Borovcanin boarded ten Muslim boys onto the bus and sent them on to Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, General, I did not record that, and I'm sorry about it, but this is what I was talking about also earlier in court. If I was there with a crew, then the cameraman would have shot that, because the efforts would have been equally distributed. I wouldn't be in charge both of the text and the camera and everything else. Somehow I missed that, and I'm very sorry because then you would see the end. As it is, you are left with my absolute assertion that all the boys from that location on that afternoon, the 13th of July, 1995, boarded lorries and buses which were already transporting people whom I partly filmed at the beginning of my report at the DutchBat compound in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. You said here that you saw a report in which he gave an account that was somewhat different to the actual events. Do you know, if you followed this trial, that there were witnesses here from this location who also said that they were the only ones who boarded a bus, only two of them, and who never said that there were ten of them? They said that there were only two of them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, I don't know who these witnesses are. I have not heard this. But I was there. Among the exhausted Muslim fighters were boys aged between 14, 15, or 17 at the most, and I remember that there were around ten of them. Once again, I can tell you that I'm very sorry that I did not film this. I was not thinking that we would be discussing this one day, and this is a great minus of my report, so what remains is just my oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Several times during the examination-in-chief you were asked about what you were saying during the filming. In part of one of your answers to the Prosecutor, you said that sometimes a cameraman says something just to fit into the conversation or to elicit a comment from the others. Did you have a feeling that I had while I was listening to it, that you are now being charged of something that you said in this footage and on the other hand you provided the basic documents which are important for the Prosecutor's Office? So are you being charged with having said something that is criminal in nature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps your remark is partly inappropriate, but I had a very decent and fruitful meeting with Mr. Vanderpuye. I have known Mr. McCloskey for quite a long time, and I don't think that they aimed at accusing me of saying something criminal. But in the text from the raw footage, I was really the one who spoke most dirtily, so perhaps it could be wrongly interpreted that I was against all Muslims, but I think I have clarified this, and I think that the Prosecutor quite understood what I wanted to say by these comments. Those, still, from this perspective, at certain moments it may look really sharp. But the situation in which this was spoken was the war, and this was not included in the final version of my report. I was for a long time accused in Belgrade and Serbia of having erased certain sections, and I could have erased this as well. But I was honest in depicting the entire atmosphere which includes this detail, and I think that the Court values this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are running out of time. It's 7.00 we have to adjourn for the day, and you may continue your cross-examination tomorrow. Sir, we have to break now for today. You should be reminded it's not allowed to have any contact to any party about the content of your testimony. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 2.15 in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of May, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
